Overview
We are Chia Network Inc., a software company focused on creating modular pieces of code that act as
accelerants to integrate the Chia blockchain into real-world applications. Through the creation of modular software,
the Chia platform enables the creation of “One Market,” a forum where developers can build global trading markets
that leverage the tools and attributes of blockchain technology to increase market efficiency. The Chia blockchain
serves as the infrastructure layer of this One Market. We built the Chia platform to drive real-world adoption of
blockchain technology. The internet enabled large-scale efficiency gains by allowing for nearly instantaneous
communication and information sharing around the globe, but users were required to trust the authenticity of
information shared, and there was no digitally native financial transaction infrastructure. Blockchain technology can
expand on the revolution of the internet by further increasing efficiencies while also strengthening trust in the
systems that provide information and enable transactions. Existing blockchain solutions have been widely studied,
but not broadly adopted, for enterprise and government use cases due to a myriad of security, ownership, and
information protection concerns. We believe blockchain technology enables collaboration and transactions without
expensive intermediaries in currently opaque markets. Blockchain technology is being used in various markets
including carbon, payments, automobile finance and titles, agriculture, securities, supply chain, and royalty-based
creator economies. We believe the Chia blockchain is the first public, highly secure, sustainable, compliant,
auditable, and currency-agnostic solution for enterprises, governments, and developers seeking to use blockchain
technology in real-world applications.
The Chia blockchain is an open source blockchain, similar to Bitcoin or Ethereum, but it is purposefully
designed to be secure, sustainable, and compliant. Although Chia Network built and continues to build on top of the
Chia blockchain, we do not own, operate, or control the Chia blockchain. Chia Network releases open source
modules aimed at making it easier and more secure for individuals to interface with the Chia blockchain. We believe
that by increasing the accessibility and capabilities of the Chia blockchain and, by extension, increasing the user
base, more expansive and complex projects will be drawn to the Chia blockchain and will require the services of
Chia Network to develop, implement, maintain, and support those projects. The Chia blockchain’s secure
environment allows for agreements to be converted to code and their execution to be automated based upon the
status of the blockchain (commonly referred to as smart contracting), resulting in the completion of transactions in a
reliable and auditable fashion. Additionally, transactions completed on the Chia blockchain are currency agnostic,
which means digital currencies besides the Chia blockchain native currency, XCH, can be used for transactions on
the Chia blockchain. The Chia blockchain also utilizes a fraction of the energy of Bitcoin and is more decentralized
than Bitcoin and Ethereum based on number of nodes and Nakamoto Coefficient. We believe that the Chia
blockchain is compliant with U.S. federal securities laws because we believe XCH is not a security and is instead
subject to the anti-manipulation and anti-fraud regulations applicable to commodities that are enforceable by the
Commodity Futures Trading Commission (“CFTC”). We expect that enterprises, governments, and developers will
use XCH to issue new Chia Asset Tokens (“CATs”), issue asset titles as non-fungible tokens (“NFTs”) in
accordance with existing regulation, or purchase goods or services. Further, the Chia blockchain offers a compliance
framework for users who can use Chia platform primitives like decentralized identifiers (“DIDs”) and verifiable
credentials to comply with their applicable regulations.

Select Use Cases of Blockchain Technology
Blockchain technology offers numerous benefits to enterprises, governments, developers, and individuals,
including improved efficiency, transparency, and security, as well as self-ownership of data and assets. We believe
there are many real-world applications that require or are materially improved by blockchain technology.
Markets: Trustworthy, Inclusive, and Global Trading
A secure and sustainable blockchain featuring a trust-enhancing smart contract environment empowers
enterprises, governments, and developers to create markets and rapidly tap into global trading liquidity. Blockchain
technology enables the trading of assets among two or more entities anywhere in the world at any time and in a way
that reduces the ability of one party to defraud another. It makes completing a trade more trustworthy and fast.
Process Integrity: Transparent, Trustless Tracking
Blockchains are excellent transparency engines. For practical reasons, tension arises when considering whether
to run a private blockchain versus a public blockchain. A project benefits from the core elements of a public
3

blockchain, like transparency and an immutable, append-only nature; however, many projects need partial or total
confidentiality. We built our DataLayer technology with these needs in mind. Leveraging the DataLayer technology,
participants can be pseudonymous to the outside world and transparent (or not) internally. Users can also prove
inclusion of select elements in a joint database selectively or publicly.
Identity: Digital Identification and Credentialing
Blockchain technology provides the opportunity for scalable and trusted DID infrastructure. Users can obtain
credentials through their DID, which could allow access to or certification of information such as a passport, trade
license, investor accreditation, or NFT authorship. This infrastructure enables DID login, a replacement for web2
logins, enterprise email access, etc. By removing the need for trusted third parties, DID helps secure identity and
enable single sign-on.
Custody: Security and Control
Blockchain technology allows for ownership of digital assets, which comes with the responsibility of security
and control. Even today’s best practices are not user friendly and are prone to user error or theft. Advancement in
blockchain technology has made it possible to mitigate the risk of unauthorized transfers or loss of money by
building safety nets directly into the software.
Payments: Democratizing Infrastructure
According to McKinsey, the cost of moving money in 2020 was approximately $915 billion. Existing payment
systems are dated, require counterparty trust, and are increasingly complex for cross-border transactions. For
example, “simple” domestic debit card transactions require end users to trust sellers, card networks, merchant and
cardholder banks, and Fedwire or ACH to achieve final settlement. Advances in blockchain technology and smart
contract capabilities have enabled trustless payments. With blockchain technology, payments can be available to
anyone, anywhere, 24×7, and settle transparently with finality in just a few minutes.
Randomness and Gaming: Predictable Unpredictability
Blockchains are a source of publicly verifiable random numbers. Sports drafts, lotteries, and on-chain games of
skill can be provably secure using blockchain technology. When the source of randomness can be trusted, corruption
becomes difficult.

The Chia Blockchain
We initially developed the Chia blockchain over a period of four years and during that time we had control over
the Chia blockchain. Following the launch of the Chia blockchain in March 2021, we ceased to have control over the
Chia blockchain as it began running independently on farmer nodes operating the Chia blockchain protocol and the
consensus mechanism contained in the Chia blockchain software. As the Chia blockchain is a decentralized public
blockchain, we do not own, operate, or control, directly or indirectly, the Chia blockchain and we cannot control,
directly or indirectly, its usage, including the publication of CATs, NFTs, or decentralized applications (“dApps”).
The node software, as agreed upon by over 50% of the nodes on the Chia blockchain, is what ultimately determines

the rules for the creation and reward of the next block. The Chia blockchain’s rules are determined by each node
operator and that limits what farmers can propose in blocks. A block seen as valid by a majority of the nodes will
generally get included as long as it is otherwise on the chain with the most space also agreeing with those rules. We
or any community member can propose to materially enhance or change components of the Chia blockchain and/or
the Chia platform. We propose enhancements and improvements to the Chia blockchain through updates to our
software and have influence on the Chia blockchain, but any upgrades have to be downloaded and installed by a
majority of farmers in order to be implemented. We do not operate any farmer nodes and, pursuant to our internal
policies, our personnel are not permitted to run farmer nodes on hardware owned or provided by us to ensure that we
do not have direct or indirect control over the Chia blockchain. The acceptance of changes proposed by us or the
community requires the majority of farmers to adopt the changes. We are not able to control or implement changes
unilaterally.

GLOSSARY
Throughout this prospectus, we use a number of industry terms and concepts which are defined as follows:
• Asset Tokens: Blockchain instruments that represent unique whole or partial ownership of a separate
physical or digital asset, deriving its value in part or whole from the represented asset. A “CAT” is a Chia
Asset Token.
• Advanced Research Projects Agency Network (“ARPANET”): The first public, wide-area packet-
switched network, and one of the first networks to implement the TCP/IP protocol suite, forming the
technical foundation of the modern internet.
• Application Specific Integrated Circuits (“ASICs”): Integrated circuits purpose built for a specific or
single use, such as voice recording or digital asset mining.
• Blocks: Synonymous with digital pages in a ledger. Blocks are added to an existing blockchain as
transactions occur on the network.
• Blockchain: A constantly growing shared database where items may be added but never changed. Records
are organized and added into the database in grouped sets called blocks and may represent items such as
transferring assets from one person to another, purchasing goods, or swapping one asset for another. In
addition to these records of change, each block contains a timestamp, a summary of events taking place
(Merkle trees), and the prior block’s unique identifier (i.e., cryptographic hash). A cryptographic hash is
created by an algorithm that can translate data input into a fixed-size output of encrypted text. These hash
functions are used in each block to generate its unique identifier. Each function takes in as input its own
timestamp, the prior block’s events, and the prior block’s identifier. This allows for the creation of a
sequential system database, which is important because a change to any given block would only be possible
if every block before it was able to be altered as well.
• Blockchain Trilemma: The industry-accepted concept that a Layer 1 blockchain can be only two of fast,
decentralized, or secure. The term was coined by Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin and is widely
accepted as a fundamental blockchain design concept. At the current stage of blockchain technology
development and innovation, it is not possible for a Layer 1 blockchain to be fast (have a high amount of
transactions per second), decentralized, and secure because increasing two of the three properties results in
weakening the third property. While developers are attempting to solve the trilemma by experimenting with
scalability and other solutions, no workable solution within a Layer 1 blockchain has been developed. We
believe such solution would require a fundamental innovation in computer science. The Chia blockchain
optimizes security and decentralization, limiting block space, which limits speed on Layer 1. In order to
allow for higher transactions per second and address the limitations of the blockchain trilemma, we intend
to leverage various net settlement Layer 2 technology scaling solutions, like payment channels and rollups.
We create primitives for use on the Chia blockchain that we anticipate developers will be able to use to
implement Layer 2 technologies for specific applications like payments, peer-to-peer gaming, and Offer
settlements.
• Carbon Credit: A transferable instrument certified by governments or independent certification bodies to
represent an emission reduction of one metric ton of CO
2
.
• Carbon Offset: Any activity that compensates for the emission of carbon dioxide or other greenhouse
gases by providing for an emission reduction elsewhere.
• Central Bank Digital Currency (“CBDC”): Digital currencies issued by a country’s central bank, with a
value and circulation controlled, directly or indirectly, by the central bank and pegged to the country’s fiat
currency.
• Chialisp Virtual Machine (“CLVM”): The Chia blockchain’s secure runtime computing environment that
deploys and executes smart contracts written in Chialisp. CLVM allows smart contract execution to be
15

automated based upon the status of the Chia blockchain, resulting in the completion of transactions in a
reliable and auditable manner. It is similar in function to the Ethereum Virtual Machine.
• Cold Wallet: A type of wallet that stores private keys offline and is not connected to the internet. Cold
wallets typically use a hardware security module such as a Secure Element, USB, or smart card, but also
include paper-based wallets and managed cold storage services.
• Consensus Mechanism: A set of ideas, incentives, protocols, and social constructs that enable a distributed
set of nodes or validators to agree on, or “validate,” the current state of a blockchain.
• Decentralized Application (“dApp”): Any application whose core elements are a blockchain and code-
based execution.
• Decentralized Exchange (“DEX”): A peer-to-peer bulletin board that enables transactions to take place
without a centralized intermediary such as a bank or broker.
• Epoch: In Ethereum, a group of 32 slots that present a 6.4-minute average window of opportunity for
validators to propose blocks for a series of transactions.
• Ethereum Request for Comment 20 (“ERC-20”): The technical standard for fungible tokens created on
the Ethereum blockchain that allows developers to build smart-contract-enabled tokens.
• Ethereum Request for Comment 721 (“ERC-721”): The technical standard for non-fungible tokens
created on the Ethereum blockchain that allows developers to build unique, non-replicable digital tokens.
• Farming: The process of validating and being rewarded in XCH by the Chia blockchain protocol for
validating transactions on the Chia blockchain through the Proof of Space and Time consensus mechanism.
Users who engage in farming are called “farmers.”
• Federated Database: A database management system that helps to map multiple autonomous databases.
• Finality: The agreed upon methodology of determining that a block can no longer be manipulated by a bad
actor using a short-range attack.
• GitHub Stars: A metric available on public Git repository GitHub whereby users “star” open source
projects and repositories to bookmark them and show appreciation for the project developer’s work, in turn
serving as both an indicator of popularity and a proxy for frequency of use.
• Hash Function: A function that converts and assigns a given numeric or alphanumeric value of arbitrary
size into a small and practical fixed-size integer value.
• Hot Wallet: A type of software wallet that stores public and private keys online and connected to the
internet. Hot wallets are typically accessed through a computer web browser, smartphone, or third-party
centralized exchanges and emphasize access and convenience in performing transactions.
• Layer 1: The foundational code that defines the rules of a blockchain.
• Layer 2: A second layer of code that that can be used to expand the functionality of a Layer 1 blockchain.
Layer 2 blockchains are generally scaling solutions that include payment channels, rollups, and net
settlement.
• Maximal Extractable Value (“MEV”): The maximum excess value over the base block reward and
transaction fees that can be extracted by a validator on a given blockchain.
• Mempool: A staging area for signed transactions awaiting confirmation for inclusion in a block.
• Merkle Trees: A data structure used for data verification and synchronization.
16

• Mining: The process of validating and being rewarded for validating transactions through the Proof of
Work consensus mechanism on blockchains such as Bitcoin, based on the amount of compute power
allocated. Users who engage in mining are called “miners.”
• Multi-signature Delayed Transactions: Transactions that require the consent of multiple parties as well as
the passage of a defined amount of time.
• Nakamoto Coefficient: A measure of the smallest number of nodes or entities that could collude and reach
the minimum threshold needed to exercise control over, significantly hinder the finality of, or launch a
successful attack on a blockchain.
• Nakamoto Consensus: The Nakamoto Consensus is a set of rules that verifies the authenticity of a
blockchain network using a rule that selects the blockchain that has had the most work completed. This is
the approach to verification used by Bitcoin and the Chia blockchain.
• Node: A device authorized to keep track of the distributed ledger and serve as a communication hub for
various network tasks.
• Nonce: An abbreviation of “number only used once,” a nonce is the number that blockchain validators are
solving for in a Proof of Work consensus mechanism.
• Non-fungible Token (“NFT”): Any unique piece of data that lives on a blockchain as code. This can be
contrasted with a cryptocurrency, which is an example of a “fungible token” and can be used
interchangeably with other cryptocurrencies of the same type.
• One Market: Today, markets are often opaque and siloed just as information was before the advent of the
internet. We believe blockchains have the capacity to bring to finance and trading markets the same kind of
broad discoverability, ease of access, and interoperability that web2 brought to information generally. This
“One Market” is a forum where any issuer or dApp provider can build a global 24x7 trading market for its
assets that leverages existing liquidity, uses on-chain trading tools that provide for trustless settlement that
does not require escrow, increases trust by requiring fewer intermediaries, and improves discoverability,
auditability, and authenticity, all of which leads to increased market efficiency.
• Pooling: The aggregation of resources by validators to increase the probability of being selected as a miner.
• Primitive: In the context of software development, a basic interface or piece of code that can be used to
build more complex or targeted applications.
• Pre-plotted Recycled Drive: Recycled hard drives that come pre-filled with cryptographic data, offering
plug-and-play, sustainable, and low barriers-to-entry for farming on the Chia blockchain.
• Protocol: A type of algorithm or software that governs how a blockchain operates.
• Public Blockchain, Private Blockchain: Public blockchains are accessible to anyone, while private
blockchains are accessible to only select users.
• Private Key: Each public address has a corresponding public key and private key that are cryptographically
generated. A private key allows the key holder to access any funds belonging to the address, similar to a
bank account password. A public key helps validate transactions that are broadcasted to and from the
address. Addresses are shortened versions of public keys, which are derived from private keys.
• Raspberry Pi: A series of low-cost computers with minimal compute power, produced originally for
education purposes.
• Scaling Solutions: Technological solutions that help blockchains to process more transactions per second,
including Layer 2 blockchains, also known as “sidechains,” cryptographic consolidation of transactions off
the blockchain, also known as “rollups,” and communication protocols between participants, also known as
“state channels.”
17

• Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (“SHA-256”): A deterministic unkeyed cryptographic hash that converts
inputs of variable length into a 256-bit hash output and is used in blockchains to ensure that no one can
tamper with the previously agreed upon transaction history.
• Slots: Intervals of approximately 12 seconds in Proof of Stake blockchains when validators have the
opportunity to build and propose a block.
• Smart Contract: Software that digitally facilitates or enforces a rules-based agreement or terms between
transacting parties.
• Stablecoin: Digital assets with a pegged value, tracking the price of another asset such as a fiat currency,
commodity, or financial instrument, for a lower volatility digital currency that is more suited to everyday
use.
• Staking: An energy efficient replacement for mining. Stakers use pools of tokens as collateral to validate
transactions and create blocks. In exchange for this service, stakers earn a reward.
• Tokenization: In the context of blockchain, tokenization refers to the creation of blockchain-based digital
assets.
• Validator: Someone who is responsible for verifying transactions on a blockchain.
• Verifiable Delay Function (“VDF”): A function that requires a specified number of sequential steps to
evaluate and which has a publicly and rapidly verifiable output. VDFs are most commonly used to ensure
that a specified amount of time passes, based on currently available compute capabilities, before an event
occurs.
• Voluntary Carbon Market: The market where carbon emitters and projects that remove or reduce
greenhouse gases from the atmosphere can buy or sell carbon offsets and carbon credits.
• Wallet: A place to store public and private keys for digital assets. Wallets are typically software, hardware,
or paper based.
• Wallet Address: An alphanumeric reference to a wallet where digital assets can be sent or stored.
• Warm Wallet: A term we use to describe one kind of wallet that holds a portion of our Strategic Reserve.
Warm wallets are functionally identical to cold wallets – the hardware security module is offline and never
connected to the internet; however, the warm wallets require fewer signatures and the required length of
delay between spends and the length of clawbacks are measured in hours instead of days. Our warm wallets
use the same technologies as our cold wallets.

changes in ownership among stockholders considered by the rules as owning, directly or indirectly, 5% or more of
the stock of a corporation, as well as changes in ownership arising from new issuances of stock by the corporation.

which may be outside of our control, may result in an ownership change under these rules.

except that NOLs generated in 2018, 2019, and 2020 may be carried back to each of the five tax years preceding the

Chia Blockchain Metrics:
Average Utilization of Block Space. The utilization of block space represents the average data usage within a
given block during a specified time period. It is similar to number of transactions, but it takes into account the
complexity of transaction types. Therefore, the utilization of block space is representative of user engagement with
applications on and demand for the Chia blockchain. We believe there is a direct correlation between the utilization
of block space and the demand for blockchain resources. In the short to medium term, we expect the average
utilization of block space to increase as demand for the Chia blockchain increases. We expect the growth rate of the
average utilization of block space to slow as users become more efficient in their usage and begin to implement
scaling solutions, which are technological solutions that help blockchains process more transactions per second. In
the long term, we expect that the average utilization of block space will remain high, reflecting the strong demand.
In a given period, the average utilization of block space can be volatile due to a project being launched or other
factors, such as holidays when the Chia blockchain community tends to be more active. For example, the seven-day
period ending December 31 tends to show higher-than-normal average utilization of block space.
We calculate the average utilization of block space on the Chia blockchain by averaging the utilization of block
space for every day in the seven-day period ending on the date of measurement. By using the average over this
period, we smooth the data and the usage volatility that occurs in the course of a week. The average utilization of
block space on the Chia blockchain was 4.3% and 5.5% as of March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023, respectively, a
decrease of 20%.
We believe this decrease was due to unusually high activity on the Chia blockchain related to users inserting
inscriptions, which are a novel way of including data in the form of code, image, audio, and text files in a
blockchain, following the sudden popularity of Ordinals on the Bitcoin blockchain. Bitcoin Ordinals inspired similar
temporary increased activity across a number of Layer 1 blockchains, including the Chia blockchain. The significant
volume driven by inscription activity appears to have ended shortly before the measurement window on March 22,
2024 after reaching a sustained approximately 45% average utilization over a three week period from December 23,
2023 through January 14, 2024. Utilization remained in the range of 11.3% to 35.2% between January 17, 2024 and
March 19, 2024. We believe that the utilization of block space has stabilized to be in line with pre-inscriptions
activity since then.
Average Fees Paid per Block. While average utilization of block space is a metric of demand, average fees
paid per block in XCH takes into account the value of transacting on the Chia blockchain. Fees paid per block
comprise all transaction fees paid by requesters of transactions that are included in a given block. We believe that as
the average utilization of block space approaches 100%, the average fees paid per block to farmers by the ecosystem
will rise and lower relative value transactions will move to scaling solutions in order to increase efficiency and
reduce cost. We expect the average fees paid per block to generally increase over time.
We calculate the average fees paid per block on the Chia blockchain by averaging the total fees paid per block
for every day in the seven-day period ending on the date of measurement. By using the average over this period, we
smooth the data and the usage volatility that occurs in the course of a week. The average fees paid per block on the
Chia blockchain were 0.00145 XCH and 0.00037 XCH as of March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023, respectively, an
increase of 291%.
Average Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient. The Nakamoto Consensus is a set of rules that verifies the
authenticity of a blockchain network using a rule that selects the blockchain that has had the most work completed.
This is the approach to verification used by Bitcoin and the Chia blockchain. On the Chia blockchain, the Nakamoto
Coefficient is a measure of the smallest number of nodes that could collude and reach the greater than 50% threshold
needed to launch a successful attack on the Chia blockchain. We calculate the Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient by
counting the unique number of farmer public keys required to control more than 50% of the netspace currently
online and dedicated by farmers to the Chia blockchain over a period of time and adding back the number of unique
farmer public keys that utilize GigaHorse plot farming services. While it is possible that a farmer on the Chia
blockchain may have more than one public key, resulting in overcounting the number of farmers and thus
overestimating the Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient of the Chia blockchain, for one farmer to have more than one
public key is difficult and inefficient as they would have to re-plot any space that they had previously plotted to an
78

existing public key, and managing multiple public keys on a farm takes additional effort. Therefore, we do not
believe it is likely that many farmers have more than one public key and, if they do, it is likely that such number is
de minimis. For additional detail about the Nakamoto Coefficient for Bitcoin and for Ethereum as well as a
discussion of the limitations and potential manipulability of the Nakamoto Coefficient based on consensus
mechanism, see the section titled “Blockchain 101—Evaluation of Consensus Mechanisms.” As the Nakamoto
Coefficient rises, it represents increased decentralization of validation and increased security of the blockchain. We
generally expect the average Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient for the Chia blockchain will be consistently high and
slowly increase, and we do not expect it to oscillate significantly period over period, absent an unexpected
technological innovation. We generally expect that the increases in the average Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient for
the Chia blockchain will be due to new farmers joining the Chia blockchain and very early farmers re-plotting their
space to optimize their farming rewards potential and migrating to the current decentralized pooling protocol.
We calculate average Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient for the Chia blockchain by averaging the Adjusted
Nakamoto Coefficient for every day in the seven-day period ending on the date of measurement. By using the
average over this period, we smooth the data and the statistical noise that occurs within the course of a week. The
average Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient on the Chia blockchain was 6 and 92 as of March 31, 2024 and March 31,
2023, respectively, a decrease of 93%.
We believe this decrease was due to the rapid adoption of plot compression software that did not implement the
standard pooling protocol on the Chia blockchain, which means that actions undertaken by farmers in the pool
appear to be done by the pool itself rather than all of the individual farmers participating in the pool. We expect the
average Adjusted Nakamoto Coefficient to slowly increase due to additional third-party plot compression
technologies that are similar or superior and do utilize the standard pooling protocol.
Average Node Count. Average node count is an indicator of the security and ease of use of the Chia
blockchain. The higher the node count, the more relatively secure a blockchain is against attacks. While it is possible
for an individual or entity to create more than one node, such a process would be an inefficient use of resources
since running another node duplicates power usage and capital expenditures for farmers. Therefore, we do not
believe it is likely that any individual or entity accounts for more than one node and, if they do, it is likely that such
number is de minimis. We believe this because the vast majority of nodes on the Chia blockchain are run by farmers
and there are only a handful of services that run more than one node for redundancy and fault tolerance. We expect
average node count to be generally consistent and to increase slightly over time as the number of farmers and
implementations increase. In a given period, average node count may temporarily decrease due to external effects,
such as Microsoft Windows software updates, regional increases in electricity costs, and the volatility in the market
price of XCH.
We calculate average node count on the Chia blockchain by averaging the node count for every day in the five-
day period ending on the date of measurement. We use the industry standard five-day period because not every node
is visible to every farmer every day and because IP addresses update every 24 hours in certain regions. The average
node count on the Chia blockchain was 89,384 and 120,208 as of March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023, respectively,
a decrease of 25%.
We believe this decrease was due to consolidation and the rapid adoption of plot compression software that did
not implement the standard pooling protocol on the Chia blockchain, which means that farmer nodes in the pool
appear to be a single pool itself rather than all of the farmer nodes participating in the pool.
We ran 31 nodes and 45 nodes as of March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023, respectively, but those nodes are not
required for the Chia blockchain to function, and we may stop running nodes at any time. Our nodes are deployed

• We ran six nodes, two nodes in each of the Amazon Web Services locations found in London, Oregon, and
Tokyo as an alternative way for a new node to connect to the network.
• An additional 11 nodes supported ten Timelords distributed around the world as the Chia blockchain needs
at least one Timelord running to proceed. In May 2024, we completed a distribution of Timelord ASICs to

approximately 40 community members to add significant additional redundancy and shorter network
distances for generating Proofs of Time.
• We ran six nodes to support our internal testing and monitoring of the Chia blockchain as we have internal

• The final eight nodes are used to continuously test syncing new versions of the Chia blockchain node

Based on IP addresses, there is no geographic concentration of nodes as of March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023.
Average Total Netspace of the Chia Blockchain. The total netspace of the Chia blockchain represents the
total amount of storage being utilized by nodes to participate in PoST on the Chia blockchain. As this figure rises,
the chance that a greater than 50% attack could be launched from the outside diminishes due to supply constraints
and demand competition for unused storage; therefore, average total netspace is also a measure of the overall
security of the Chia blockchain. We monitor the total netspace of the Chia blockchain in connection with the amount
of storage that is for sale on a monthly basis as of the date of measurement because total netspace multiplied by the
cost per unit of storage indicates how costly an outside attack on the Chia blockchain would be. We expect the
average total netspace of the Chia blockchain to increase if the value of XCH increases because farming XCH would
become more profitable.
We calculate the average total netspace of the Chia blockchain by averaging the total netspace of the Chia
blockchain for every day in the seven-day period ending on the date of measurement. By using averages over this
period, we smooth the data and the usage volatility that occurs in the course of a week. The average total netspace of
the Chia blockchain was 32.6 exbibytes (37.6 exabytes) and 21.7 exbibytes (25.0 exabytes) as of March 31, 2024
and March 31, 2023, respectively, an increase of 50%.

The Chia Strategic Reserve
In March 2021, we launched the Chia blockchain. We pre-coded, and upon launch, a third-party farmer created
(by virtue of winning the first block), the Chia Strategic Reserve, a pre-farmed “genesis” block of 21 million XCH
owned by the company. We have not directly or indirectly farmed any XCH, nor have we added XCH to our
Strategic Reserve since its creation. From March 2021 until October 2023, we did not sell, gift, loan, collateralize, or
otherwise dispose of any of the XCH in our Strategic Reserve.
In October 2023, we began making sales of XCH from our Strategic Reserve. As of March 31, 2024, we have
made 350,000 XCH, or less than 1.7% of coins from our initial Strategic Reserve, available to a third-party market
maker to provide liquidity and to sell XCH on our behalf in blind programmatic transactions. From October 2023
through March 31, 2024, we made available between 50,000 and 150,000 XCH, or less than 1% of coins from our
initial Strategic Reserve, to a third-party market maker to provide liquidity on non-U.S. third-party exchanges that
are not available to persons in the United States: Gate.io, KuCoin, MEXC, and OKX Exchange. During that period,
we also sold a total of 270,174.35 XCH, or less than 1.3% of coins from our initial Strategic Reserve, in blind
programmatic transactions through the same third-party market maker on the same non-US third-party exchanges.
Pursuant to a services agreement, the third-party market maker provides liquidity services for a set monthly retainer
and earns a set service fee for any XCH sales on our behalf. All transactions completed by the third-party market
maker are completed at the market price at the time of execution of the transaction on each third-party exchange and
such transactions are completed pursuant to each exchange’s terms and conditions. We do not have contractual
privity with any such exchange for these transactions.

alternative financing, and, at that time, possibly discontinue sales of XCH or continue sales of XCH from our
Strategic Reserve to a lesser extent. While we make available XCH to a third-party market maker to provide
liquidity services and make sales of XCH from our Strategic Reserve, we have no immediate plans to sell, distribute,

Components of Results of Operations
Revenue
Revenue from Professional Services
At present, we expect to derive a large portion of our revenue from implementation services. To date, we have
derived revenue from professional services primarily for development, testing, and deployment of various
applications on the Chia Blockchain. These implementations utilize existing primitives and tools available to all
users of the Chia blockchain, including our on-chain smart contracting language, to build and provide a particular
application or service for our customers. Going forward, we expect that we will generally charge implementation
fees as a fixed cost, in fiat currency, based on the size and expected complexity of an implementation. We expect
these services to include large, medium, and small implementations. Larger implementations will tie together
multiple organizations and/or individuals in trading, contract exchange, or process integrity (or a combination of
these). Medium implementations will be tailored toward a single enterprise or government level and allow the
organization to leverage the Chia blockchain for new applications. Small implementations will be geared toward
facilitating connection of enterprise and government customers in various existing applications, as well as any major
upgrades of existing customer applications, particularly to functionality of primitives. Depending on contract
structure, we generally expect to recognize implementation revenue over the life of the implementation or major
upgrade process.
Revenue from Subscription and Support
Revenue from subscription and support is recurring in nature and earned over time as we provide additional
ongoing services to our customers. To date, we have derived revenue from subscription and support primarily for
node and application hosting and support. Going forward, we expect these contracts will generally include a fixed
fee linked to the level of complexity of the support services required as well as a variable component that will
82

depend on the user base, transaction volume, revenue derived from the use case, or other relevant metrics. We
expect our subscription services to include monitoring application and blockchain health, supporting testnets and
sandboxes, ensuring data accessibility, supporting self-custody, and updating and modifying existing
implementations to ensure normal, secure, and seamless operation of applications. We expect our support services to
include on-call technical support, application integrity and repair work, compatibility testing, modifications for
blockchain updates, supporting customer self-custody, and customer training and certification. Over time, we expect
our revenue from subscription and support to become a larger component of our overall revenue mix as it grows
along with the number and scale of our customers’ projects. We expect to recognize revenue from subscription and
support as the services are provided, which would typically occur on a monthly basis for active contracts.
Costs of Revenue
Cost of Revenue from Professional Services
Cost of revenue from professional services consists of time-spent based allocations of wages, including
employee benefits paid by us and stock-based compensation of our personnel and permanent contractors involved in
implementation services, as well as any other direct costs of implementations such as non-permanent contractors,
hardware used in implementation, and other items. The cost of revenue from professional services also includes pro-
rata allocation of depreciation and amortization expenses, which was minimal in the year ended March 31, 2024.
Going forward, we expect the cost of revenue from professional services to decrease on a per implementation basis
due to the ability to reuse parts of existing applications developed for other customers in future engagements.
Cost of Revenue from Subscription and Support
The cost of revenue from subscription and support includes time-spent based allocation of wages, including
employee benefits paid by us and stock-based compensation of our personnel involved in provision of these
services, as well as any other direct costs related to subscription and support services. The cost of revenue from
subscription and support also includes pro-rata allocation of depreciation and amortization expenses. Going forward,
we expect to realize economies of scale in the cost of revenue from subscription and support.

Select Use Cases of Blockchain Technology
Blockchain technology offers numerous benefits to enterprises, governments, developers, and individuals,
including improved efficiency, transparency, and security, as well as self-ownership of data and assets. We believe
there are many real-world applications that require or are materially improved by blockchain technology.
Markets: Trustworthy, Inclusive, and Global Trading
A secure and sustainable blockchain featuring a trust-enhancing smart contract environment empowers
enterprises, governments, and developers to create markets and rapidly tap into global trading liquidity. Blockchain
technology enables the trading of assets among two or more entities anywhere in the world at any time and in a way
that reduces the ability of one party to defraud another. It makes completing a trade more trustworthy and fast.
Process Integrity: Transparent, Trustless Tracking
Blockchains are excellent transparency engines. For practical reasons, tension arises when considering whether
to run a private blockchain versus a public blockchain. A project benefits from the core elements of a public
blockchain, like transparency and an immutable, append-only nature; however, many projects need partial or total
confidentiality. We built our DataLayer technology with these needs in mind. Leveraging the DataLayer technology,
participants can be pseudonymous to the outside world and transparent (or not) internally. Users can also prove
inclusion of select elements in a joint database selectively or publicly.
Identity: Digital Identification and Credentialing
Blockchain technology provides the opportunity for scalable and trusted DID infrastructure. Users can obtain
credentials through their DID, which could allow access to or certification of information such as a passport, trade
license, investor accreditation, or NFT authorship. This infrastructure enables DID login, a replacement for web2
logins, enterprise email access, etc. By removing the need for trusted third parties, DID helps secure identity and
enable single sign-on.
Custody: Security and Control
Blockchain technology allows for ownership of digital assets, which comes with the responsibility of security
and control. Even today’s best practices are not user friendly and are prone to user error or theft. Advancement in
blockchain technology has made it possible to mitigate the risk of unauthorized transfers or loss of money by
building safety nets directly into the software.
Payments: Democratizing Infrastructure
According to McKinsey, the cost of moving money in 2020 was approximately $915 billion. Existing payment
systems are dated, require counterparty trust, and are increasingly complex for cross-border transactions. For
example, “simple” domestic debit card transactions require end users to trust sellers, card networks, merchant and
cardholder banks, and Fedwire or ACH to achieve final settlement. Advances in blockchain technology and smart
contract capabilities have enabled trustless payments. With blockchain technology, payments can be available to
anyone, anywhere, 24×7, and settle transparently with finality in just a few minutes.

We believe the advent of blockchain technology is similar to that of the internet. Innovation of a new
technology infrastructure takes time, and broad adoption requires technology maturation and cultural acceptance.
ARPANET, the first version of the internet, delivered its first node-to-node contact in 1969, but it was not until 1994
that the first commercial transaction took place online: the sale of a Sting CD. In 1994, few imagined they would
ever purchase a car or a home online, and now there are many companies built around both of those markets. The

efficiently as well as cultural comfort around transacting online, especially for large purchases.
Technology innovations ensuring the secure transfer of information (e.g., personal information and credit card
numbers) and reliable processing of payments were some of the key milestones in the advancement of the internet.
Additional barriers to early adoption included scalability to support large transaction volume, standardization of
internet protocols, interoperability between systems and devices, and easy-to-use interfaces. Cultural acceptance was
built over time as technology evolved to address consumer needs, slowly building confidence in the system. One of
the reasons why confidence in the internet took so much time to become an ingrained part of society is because it
requires trust in multiple entities, intermediaries, and counterparties, even for simple transactions.
Blockchain technology, dApp development, and adoption are developing at a much faster pace thanks to the

Challenges to Enterprise and Government Adoption of a Public Blockchain
We believe that the core elements a secure public blockchain must possess to drive enterprise and government
adoption are smart contracting, decentralized validators, regulatory compliance tools and environmental
sustainability. We believe the lack of these core elements has limited adoption of public blockchains by enterprises
and governments.
• Secure Smart Contracting Environment. The smart contracting environment sits at the center of the
blockchain development ecosystem. We believe that when enterprises and governments decide which
environment to use, they consider security, auditability, and developer awareness. Even though the smart
contracting environment is mission critical to the blockchain, blockchain projects to date have focused
more on developer adoption. For example, Ethereum was the first to offer smart contracting environments
through its programming language, Solidity. Solidity, which was derived from JavaScript, however,
optimizes for widescale developer adoption at the cost of decreased security and auditability.
• Decentralization of Validators. If validation methodologies are centralized, enterprise and government
adoption may be limited as customers and developers would have to trust a small number of validators. In
addition, without sufficient decentralization, by number and concentration, that is not overly burdensome
on the environment, scaled use cases become economically or environmentally irresponsible. To date, the
two most popular mechanisms by which blockchains agree or disagree on the inclusion of transactions in
blocks (the consensus mechanism) are Proof of Stake and Proof of Work. Proof of Work is largely
considered an environmentally unsustainable solution due to the energy usage required and e-waste
generated from single-use semiconductors. Proof of Stake generally fails due to a “rich get richer” issue
where the more of the staked cryptocurrency a validator holds, the more of it a validator generates.
Additionally, staking is often accomplished using pools of capital, which require users to delegate voting
power to the large staking entities providing the pool. This centralization of power results in decreased trust
in the system.
• Compliance Tools and Coin Compliance. Compliance is a necessity for enterprise and government
adoption. Due to the novel nature of blockchain technology, we believe many existing compliance tools do
not currently have the ability to interact with the transaction data provided by underlying blockchains,
leaving enterprises, governments, and developers to create their own tools or postpone their deployment
until new compliance tools are released. Without an ability to facilitate compliance with relevant legal and
operational frameworks, enterprise and government adoption may stall. Additionally, the native coin must
comply with applicable regulations, including U.S. securities laws and regulations.

• Sustainable Consensus Mechanism. Due to the emerging importance of ESG, enterprises and
governments want the consensus mechanism to be both economically and environmentally sustainable. For
example, Proof of Work, the consensus mechanism used by Bitcoin, requires a large amount of energy

Our Innovations
Our innovations enable secure, decentralized, compliant, and sustainable adoption of blockchain technology.
These innovations are designed to address the challenges to enterprise and government adoption of blockchain
technology and include:
• Coin model and Chialisp. There are two primary ways that blockchain databases present the data that they
store: the Account model and the Coin model. The Chia blockchain uses the Coin model. Most blockchains
use the Account model, which places a central and monolithic smart contract on the blockchain where
various capabilities and authorizations are stored in one long list. When one entity transfers an asset to
another, the smart contract itself updates its list of who owns what.
In the Coin model, which Bitcoin pioneered and the Chia blockchain and Chia platform simplified and
adopted, each item represented in the blockchain database is its own object called a “coin” that can
optionally be as intelligent as a computer because it retains knowledge of its owners and spending rules.
When a seller with a $1 coin wants to transfer $0.50 of that coin to a buyer, the buyer destroys the $1 coin
and creates two $0.50 coins. At the end of the transaction, one coin is still managed by the seller’s key and
the other by the buyer’s key. During the course of this transaction, the seller and the buyer can agree to add
restrictions and capabilities by creating small computer programs. As an example, the seller could
implement a four-hour window during which the seller can recall the $0.50 coin back to itself to protect
from a mistake in the buyer’s wallet address. This way the seller and the buyer know that the funds have
been sent, but the funds are not totally under the buyer’s control until the end of that four-hour period. Once
that predetermined period is over, the transaction is immediately final.
The Coin model is more efficient than the Account model. Instead of all participants trying to update a
popular centralized smart contract in Ethereum in each block, only the parties wishing to transact at a given
moment are making changes to the global blockchain database, and only to the specific coins used in those
parties’ transaction.
The Coin model is also more secure than the Account model. Each coin is its own copy of the smart
contract and is under the sole control of the owner. Owners can create vaults, which are themselves coins
that can hold and manage other coins that represent assets or identities. This allows the blockchain itself to
enforce a wallet’s rules that limit how much of an asset can be spent per day or how long a delay is required
when using a backup key to recover assets and identities. Centralized smart contracts in the Account model
leave control of the smart contracts in the hands of as few as one or two entities to allow for upgrades and
security fixes. The Chia platform Coin model uses Offers, which are discussed below, and multiple key
recovery to address the same issues without centralized control.
Every coin on the Chia blockchain is a Chialisp program. Lisp is a programming language that treats both
data and code as lists and excels at managing those lists. We chose to extend the programming language
Lisp because blockchains can be simplified to lists. The chain of blocks is a list where each block contains
a list of the transactions or coins that changed in that block. Blocks and transactions rely on a cryptographic
method called Merkle trees that are verifiable and auditable lists. A Chialisp coin is analogous to a
Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. Each sheet can contain both data and code that can transform that data. When
an owner interacts with a spreadsheet as coin, the owner proves that they are authorized to update the data
in that Excel spreadsheet and then the coin allows the owner to change some data or code – which is a
103

transaction. This change is then evaluated by the spreadsheet and updated into a new output spreadsheet
that then waits for the next attempt to update it.
Lisp is also extensible to application-specific uses. Chialisp brings Lisp to blockchains, adding features like
a direct way to generate a cryptographic hash or digitally sign an object. Lisp-related languages are limited
in scope, making auditing and formal verification much easier. Though coding in Lisp, and by extension
Chialisp, is initially a steep learning curve, once a developer has a handle on the basics, they can be more
productive and more capable in determining the outcomes of their smart contracts.
They are also interpreted languages, as compared to most other languages like C++ that are compiled. This
is important because we believe it limits the ability of a Chialisp coin to impact machines outside of the
validating software running it and do malicious things, such as take control of computer cameras, install
malware, or steal keys and passwords from the approximately 89,000 computers around the world that are
validating and farming as of March 31, 2024.
Due to the integration of the Coin model and Chialisp, many developers will be able to use the Chia
platform without needing to write Chialisp at all. The core primitive Chialisp coins are network-wide
standards to which a developer merely has to add their specific additions. These Chialisp objects are
composable and easily managed with applications and libraries in other languages such as Go or
Typescript. Issuing an asset and managing that asset over its lifetime can be done from a desktop or web2
application. This also means that fundamental blockchain objects that have potentially high security risks
like CATs can benefit from focused community, academic, and expert review, review by our developers,
and can be audited for increased security.
• Offers. With Offers technology, parties can trade assets or transact peer-to-peer on the Chia blockchain in a
frictionless and trustless way. An Offer includes specific parameters of a proposed transaction and a
counterparty may choose to accept the Offer, or not. If a counterparty does not accept the Offer, the
transaction does not happen. If an Offer is accepted, the specified parameters are automatically executed
with no need for trust or escrow. An Offer can be easily cancelled unless and until it is accepted into the
blockchain. Offers is not an exchange platform. Instead, users of the Chia blockchain can download wallet
software that includes Offers technology in order to engage in peer-to-peer trading of assets and execution
of transactions. Offers can be used to buy and sell XCH for a stablecoin, acquire tokenized carbon offsets
for XCH or a stablecoin, trade NFTs for other NFTs, or propose a change in a DataLayer federated
database in return for such change and a stablecoin payment.
We do not receive fees, commissions, or other payments, in the form of digital assets or other
consideration, for trades or transactions executed with Offers. As Offers is a technology implemented in
software for peer-to-peer transactions, we do not operate Offers, administer Offers, or participate in trades
or transactions conducted using Offers. We also do not and cannot limit what assets can be exchanged via
Offers.
• Parallel Block Execution. On the Chia blockchain, all transactions are completed in a block in parallel.
Transaction order matters on Ethereum and other similar blockchains. If transaction order matters,
validators can “front run” transactions for illicit profit, which is known as Maximal Extractable Value
(“MEV”). Participants on the Chia blockchain only interact with the specific coins needed for a single
transaction, thereby making the system more secure, efficient, and scalable because transactions are faster
and occur concurrently.
• DataLayer. Using DataLayer, our federated database technology, groups of enterprises, governments,
developers, and individuals can create databases that are a part of a system of databases that can reference
one another and are built on a public blockchain. This federated database system can have a range of access
controls, set by the participants of the federation, allowing for full transparency or access to only select
information. Coordination events, the pseudonymous identity of the parties, and hashes of the underlying
database contents are publicly available on the blockchain while the underlying data can be limited to each
party’s local copy of the federated database. All updates are append-only, immutable, and coordinated on

the blockchain. DataLayer thus enables multiparty collaboration where all parties have the full ability to

using iPhones and modern Android phones as hardware keys that can be used to secure vaults. This

supports and defines how to reach consensus. Members of the ecosystem are able to request changes to be made to
this software or can copy all of the code to a new repository to create their own implementation of the Chia
blockchain. We control this GitHub repository and our engineering management team reviews, approves, and
commits all software code changes in the repository. While we are not required to implement community approved
changes or requests, it is not in our best interest to ignore community feedback as there are competing forks of the
Chia blockchain, as well as competing repositories relating to all aspects of the Chia blockchain software. As of
March 31, 2024, there are over 2,000 forks of the Chia blockchain repository.
As an extreme example, if we were to ship a change that halved the farming rewards as laid out in the Chia
blockchain trailing emissions schedule, farmers on the Chia blockchain would likely not download or install the
change. Instead, most likely, a developer in our ecosystem would copy all of our software, remove the change, and
publish it as an alternative version. Once the majority of farmers install the new software as proposed by our
ecosystem developer, we would no longer be the primary software provider and the Chia blockchain would continue
to run uninterrupted and ignore all of our future updates that contained the controversial change. Already, the
Sweetchia pool of approximately 450 farmers maintains a full fork of all Chia blockchain software at most releases
so that they can support a type of pooling that the community generally does not use because it does not use newer
Advanced Custody protocols. They and other developers and farmers can easily maintain a full version of the Chia
blockchain software that does not contain any controversial change that does not have broad consensus, including
any such change from us. As such, we believe that building rough consensus among the most technically
sophisticated developers in an open manner is the best way to continue to enhance and improve the core capabilities
of the Chia blockchain.
There are many instances of an open source community choosing a different roadmap than the initial project
team. Notably, when MySQL was sold to Sun Microsystems in February 2008, the community created a carbon
copy of the MySQL code base and shipped a solution in October 2009, called MariaDB, that has been maintained to
this day and is compatible with the MySQL code base. The MariaDB example highlights the ability of a community
to create and maintain a viable alternative of an open source project separate and apart from the original creators.
In the normal course, there are two types of material changes that we or the ecosystem can request: hard forks
and soft forks. Hard forks are changes to the software that require adoption to remain compatible within the other
nodes while soft forks do not require adoption, although not adopting may minorly impact node function (e.g., there
may be transaction types that are not fully understood). Hard forks are usually foundational changes, which we
attempt to avoid, while soft forks are generally lighter upgrades to functionality, such as new types of transactions or
features. Hard and soft forks can be requested by community members or internal developers through CHIPs as
discussed below. To date, the Chia blockchain has not had a hard fork although software that contains a hard fork
was released in August 2023 and activation of the hard fork is expected in calendar year 2024 as discussed below.
Non-material changes can be requested through Pull Requests.
To ensure community consensus while not unduly slowing innovation, we utilize the following three primary
methods to decide upon and deliver changes to the chia-blockchain repository: the CHIPs process, Pull Requests,
and the high-risk security vulnerabilities process.
109

CHIPs Process
CHIPs are modeled after the Bitcoin Improvement Proposals process. We or any community member can
propose to materially enhance or change components of the Chia blockchain and/or Chia platform. Any changes or
updates to primitives like the CAT or NFT standards are published as proposed CHIPs, and company and third-party
developers comment, debate, and come to a rough consensus on whether the changes contemplated should be made.
Important or controversial issues other than high-risk security vulnerabilities are proposed via the CHIP process.
While we have a voice in the CHIPs process, we do not ultimately control the direction and consensus of the
community.
For example, advancements in GPUs and computer bus speeds could make it economically viable to attempt to
use GPUs as an alternative to storing plots, making PoST more like Proof of Work. Though this is not a security risk
to the network, it would stray from the core efficiency design of the Chia blockchain. The Chia blockchain protocol
has always envisioned that as computers continue to increase in power, the minimum size of a plot would have to
increase. This risk became evident as third-party developers shipped enhancements, independent of us, of the
standard plotting and farming capabilities of the Chia blockchain, so we proposed the first hard fork of the Chia
blockchain in response to concerns raised by the community in order to push that risk out for many years while not
requiring existing farmers on the Chia blockchain to replot to the next larger plot size now. This CHIP was accepted
by a supermajority of nodes, and we believe feedback from our community was positive.
An example soft fork proposal that activated in July 2023 is a CHIP to add the capability to make a coin not
spendable after a specified time, which is a highly requested new capability from the company and ecosystem
developers.
Community-proposed CHIPs, like company-proposed CHIPs, are subject to rigorous review by the community.
For example, CHIP-0032 was proposed by a community member in March 2024 to block the NoSSD pooling
protocol from the Chia blockchain. We did not substantially weigh in on the CHIP in order to allow community
members to debate its merits. The community feedback was overwhelmingly negative, and the community came to
the consensus that the Chia blockchain should remain permissionless without censoring transactions from NoSSD.
CHIP-0032 was withdrawn by the proposer.
Company-proposed CHIPs do not always survive community consensus building either. CHIP-0003 was a
proposal from Bram Cohen and one of our developers to implement an additional minimum transaction fee to
attempt to mitigate some spam transactions the Chia blockchain was experiencing. Our community came to the
consensus that the existing minimum fees that take effect once blocks start to fill were enough and that the benefits
of low fees in the short term offset the lesser annoyance caused by the spam. CHIP-0003 was ultimately withdrawn
and abandoned.
Pull Requests
Some changes are routine and are completed by company and community developers committing changes to the
repositories through Pull Requests. On the chia-blockchain GitHub homepage there are nine main menu items, one
of which is a tab called “Pull Requests.” On this tab, anyone can see proposed changes that do not require a CHIP
and can propose a change themselves. Once a Pull Request is created, a public comment thread is generated where
the community can comment on potential changes. Pull Requests, whether internal or external, will go through a
public comment and testing period prior to being included in the resulting code base. These changes are documented
in our release notes for each version. Examples include user interface improvements, new features enabled by new
primitives, bug fixes, medium- to low-risk security fixes, extensions to the APIs that our node and wallet provide, or
extensions of existing primitives like Offers. These are generally non-controversial and are not considered important
enough for individual CHIPs, unless they alter a standard like CAT2.
High-Risk Security Vulnerabilities Process
We handle high-risk security vulnerabilities that can lead to more than a minimal loss of funds by users of the
Chia blockchain in an alternative way. These have historically been found by our developers or our third-party
software auditors or have been submitted through our bug bounty and other responsible disclosure methods. We
110

engage third-party software auditors to audit different components of the Chia blockchain software and the Chia
platform two to three times per year, or more frequently depending on blockchain and platform developments that
were previously unaudited or have had significant changes since the last audit and our assessment of risk in such
new or changed implementations. For example, in 2022, we identified a vulnerability through a third-party software
audit on the Chia blockchain that had minimal impact on users and was mitigated by an update to the Chia
blockchain. Additionally, we engaged a third-party software auditor to review the CAT1 standard as we made
material enhancements to the original fungible token standard that was also previously audited by a third-party
software auditor in 2021. The CAT1 standard enables users to issue fungible tokens and if a material vulnerability
existed, it would potentially impact many tokens issued on the Chia blockchain and have negative financial or
reputational impacts on Chia blockchain users and us. Based on that risk assessment, we determined that a third-
party software audit was warranted. Further, for newly released software, we make a determination of whether a
material risk might be present that poses a financial or reputational risk to Chia blockchain users or the company. If
warranted, we perform the necessary software audits, including through the engagement of a third-party software
auditor. We assess such third-party audit results and determine materiality and remediation efforts based on user,
developer, or customer demand or risk.
Our developers also review the severity of any potentially high-risk security issue. If we determine that the issue
is sufficiently severe, we privately develop a fix and add it into our next release or declare a soft fork if needed. We
withhold certain details until enough farmers have updated to a version that contains the security fix. At that point in
time, we release a postmortem and explanation of the vulnerability for everyone to review. This process is meant to
protect any at-risk funds until the network has been secured by the voluntary adoption of the new version by the
farmers.
Even with high-risk security vulnerabilities, it is the farmers and users who control updates and fixes. For any
updates or fixes to the Chia blockchain to be implemented, they must be adopted by a majority of farmers and a
majority of users must download and use the updated version. For example, a majority of our farmers had upgraded
to the latest version by approximately 55 days after its release. We do not control the acceptance of any updates or
fixes, and we have not controlled the Chia blockchain since March 2021.

The wallets containing our Strategic Reserve use our Advanced Custody tools and have been customized to be
like a vault that is an autonomous wallet located on the blockchain whose restrictions are Chialisp code and whose
authorizations are managed via signatures from each individual key holder’s wallet and private key. Our Advanced
Custody tools applied to our Strategic Reserve wallets enforce certain rules, including, multiple individuals must
sign a transaction to execute it (three of five individuals for cold wallets and two of three individuals for warm
wallets), various theft hardening tools, the ability for signers to be re-keyed by other signers, and the time locks on
movements of the coin. During these time locks, spent coins can be clawed back to the original wallet address to
further protect against theft. Clawbacks are pre-set so that each economic spend will implement a clawback window
relative to the current time that the spend is submitted to the Chia blockchain. For example, if we intended to move
coins in one of the cold wallets for our Strategic Reserve to a new wallet, and we submitted the transaction on
January 1, the Chialisp of the vault would calculate and set a restriction prohibiting all movement of those coins,
except being clawed back to the sending wallet at any point during that window, until April 1 (90 days later). After
90 days, the coins can be moved immediately only to the address specified in the original spending transaction on
January 1. These Advanced Custody tools allow us to enforce our policy of giving at least 90 days’ public notice if
our plans to sell or dividend XCH from our cold wallets change. A 24 hour clawback window applies to our warm
wallets. Further, should we decide not to proceed with a transaction or determine that a transaction was started by
fraud or theft, since we retain at least backups of three of the private keys, we can clawback the coins that are in the
clawback window immediately and only to the wallet they were sent from. In addition, there are security limitations
enforced by Chialisp on the Chia blockchain that only allow a next spend to occur 30 days after the last spending
attempt from our cold wallets and one hour in the case of our warm wallets. The Advanced Custody tool settings
described above are specific to the vault wallets containing XCH from our Strategic Reserve. The Advanced
Custody tools of the Chia platform are available to any user of the Chia blockchain, and any user, farmer, or
developer can customize the specific parameters desired for their vaults and any digital assets contained within. See
the section titled “—Our Innovations.”

BLOCKCHAIN 101
A blockchain is a decentralized, distributed ledger (or database) that stores records across a network of
computers (or nodes) in a secure and transparent system. Each node holds a copy of the database, which can be
audited by the public, offering inherent security benefits. Adding a record to the ledger is commonly referred to as a
transaction. Transactions are recorded in blocks and linked together in a chain, hence the term blockchain.
The system is designed to be append only, meaning new records may be added to update information, but prior
records cannot be altered. On a blockchain, each block contains the information of all prior blocks making it nearly
impossible to alter past records. The transparent and distributed nature of a blockchain makes it a trusted way to
store digital information such as records of ownership or transactions.
A complete transaction needs three things: validation of the transaction, inclusion into a block, and the payment
of a transaction fee. The figure below illustrates a typical transaction on the blockchain.

Blockchain Data Storage: Coin Model and Account Model
There are two primary models by which blockchains store information: the Coin model and the Account model.
The type of model dictates the rules around the validation of transactions and blocks for inclusion.
The Coin model is simpler and more secure than the Account model. Validators must check previously
confirmed transactions to determine whether the user of a coin has ownership of the coin in question. If so, the
transaction can be placed into the next block and confirmed as valid by the rest of the network of validators.
The Account model is a list of owners and amounts. Transactions interact with a centralized, monolithic smart
contract (for example, smart contract standards including ERC-20 assets and ERC-721 NFTs) to alter ownership of
accounts and amounts.
The core difference between the Coin model and Account model is that transactions in the Coin model only
need access to the specific coins involved in the transaction. For example, when transacting in cash, the greatest risk
is that your cash is stolen and your goods are never delivered (risk is limited to the value you are transacting) while
the greatest risk when transacting with a debit card is that your debit card is stolen and all of your money in your
126

bank account is stolen (risk expands to the amount of capital held in the account). In this example, cash is equivalent
to the Coin model while the debit card is equivalent to the Account model. Transactions in the Account model must
interact with a smart contract that has access to all accounts and values to change the state of ownership of coins. By
extension, the Account model requires users to trust that the monolithic smart contract is not exploitable. There may
be a risk in the Account model that a contract administrator is hiding a backdoor or that hackers can find accidental
back doors. In some cases contract administrators may have complete control of the smart contract both historically
and going forward. In practice, this would allow a single party to have control over all financial value and
transactions of the affected smart contract.
In the Coin model, each validator in the network contains the previously agreed upon history of the blockchain.
The validators who are not proposing the block run the proposed list of changes paired with their history through a
cryptographic hash function. If a given validator’s hash function returns the same nonce as the proposed block, that
validator can attest that the previously agreed upon history of the blockchain is correct and was not incorrectly
altered by the block proposer. The validators will also attest that all digital signatures necessary for each transaction
to occur are correct.
Bitcoin and the Chia blockchain use the Coin model (sometimes referred to as the UTXO model for Bitcoin),
while Ethereum uses the Account model.
Interactions with the Blockchain
Users interact with a blockchain in three ways: by using a wallet to do transactions (the most common form of
interaction), by running a validator, or by using a combination of wallets and validators. Examples of interactions
with a blockchain include people buying NFTs to support their favorite creator or enterprises buying carbon credits
to offset their carbon footprints.
Wallets
For users to send and receive transactions, users must first set up a wallet. A wallet holds the user’s private key,
which is used to sign transactions, confirming that a user is in control of its digital assets. There are currently two
types of wallets: custodial and self-custodial. With a custodial wallet, a centralized entity holds the private key, and
with a self-custodial wallet, the user holds the private key. There are risks to both types of wallets. If a user with a
self-custodial wallet loses its private key, the user will lose access to its funds. Custodial wallets operate more
similarly to how banks work today, meaning the digital assets held in those wallets are assets of the user and
liabilities of the centralized entity that created the wallet. However, there is no depository insurance for digital
assets, meaning users are subject to the risk that the centralized entities remain solvent. Chia Network has sought to
127

address this issue for users of the Chia platform by creating more advanced mechanisms for self-custody that allow
for a unique system of backup wallets.
Once a user decides which type of wallet they would like to use, they get a wallet from a wallet provider’s
